text.en: What comes down but never goes up? Rain! We watch the sky for clues, collect rainwater and ask where it goes. Surya and Barkha follow the taps and pipes at home to find where the water comes from, and one day the water supply stops. This chapter is about how water reaches us, how we store and use it and how we should save it.

We can guess if it will rain by watching clues such as dark clouds, cool wind and the smell of wet earth. Elders know many clues. We can ask questions about the rain. Is it heavy or light? Are the raindrops big or small? Does it fall straight or slant in the wind? Rain can make us happy, but a heavy rain can also trouble some people.
When it rains, water falls on different surfaces. On hard surfaces it flows away or dries up in the sun, and on soil much of it soaks in. Water that soaks into the soil may slowly flow under the ground to a stream or pond. Some of it stays under the ground between the rocks and soil, and the water in our wells comes from this underground water. Streams join rivers. Water also gathers in puddles, ponds and lakes, and flows to seas and oceans. Rainwater that sinks into the soil is very important because it fills our water sources and helps plants grow.
Water is a gift of nature. It reaches our taps through pipes from a tank, and the tank is filled from a bigger source such as a river, lake or well. Some homes get water from a well or a borewell, drawn with a pulley, a hand pump or an electric pump. Some people carry water from a river or a lake, and some get it from tankers. We should thank the people who bring us water. Some families face difficulty in getting water every day.
Water is used for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, cleaning and watering plants. When the supply stops, as it did for Surya and Barkha when the society pipeline burst, the water stored in buckets helps. Long ago, there were no taps and pipes anywhere. People learned to make vessels to store water, such as clay pots, clay surahis, copper vessels and brass pots. Today we also use steel and aluminium pots, glass and plastic bottles and plastic buckets. Used water becomes dirty and cannot be used for drinking or cooking, but it can be reused for watering plants or flushing toilets. We should not add too much soap and other chemicals to water.
Water is sacred because we cannot live without it. In some places it rains very little, and people walk long distances to get water. Everyone should get clean drinking water anywhere, anytime. We can offer clean water to those who come to our door, such as postal and sanitation workers. Many places keep pots of free drinking water outside homes in the hot months. We can make a birdbath with a shallow wide container, stones for perching and fresh water, and change the water often. We can save water by closing the tap, using only the water we need and reusing water for plants.
Here is a fun activity: watch the sky every day for a week and guess whether it will rain. Your guess may be right on some days and wrong on others, and that is perfectly fine for a young scientist. Ask an elder how they guess the rain, and write at least two clues for 'it will rain today' and two for 'it will not rain today'. When it rains, ask yourself questions: is the rain heavy or light, are the drops big or small, do they fall fast or slow? Sometimes the rain is so heavy that we see lines or sheets of water instead of drops, and sometimes it slants because the wind changes its direction. Collect some rainwater in a clean vessel and look at it: does it look clean or dirty?
Think about whether it will rain again today or tomorrow, and whether it rained only in your area or in nearby places too; you can ask and find out. We can sing songs about the rain, in our own language or any other, or even make up a new one. The rain makes many people happy, but ask yourself whether it made everyone happy, because a heavy rain can trouble some people. Your teacher can do this first part of the chapter on any rainy day, so you can freely watch, question, guess, draw and record.
Is there a stream, river, pond or lake near your village or city? Find out its name and a little about it. You can visit it and draw its picture, with the trees, birds and animals that you see around it. You can also find a poem about a river and sing it in class, because water inspires many songs and stories.
Surya and Barkha followed the pipes from their taps and found a tank on the roof, and then wondered how the water came into the tank in the first place. If you get water from a tap, ask the elders at home where it comes from; they may tell you about a tank on the terrace or one some distance away. If you have a well or a borewell, watch how the water is drawn, and guess again where the water in the well comes from. If someone carries water to your home from a tap, a well, a river or a lake, say a big thank you to them.
List all the activities for which you need water, and think how many mugs you need to brush your teeth and how much water a shower uses. Think of a day when you did not get any water, and what you did then, just as Surya and Barkha did with their stored buckets.
Ask your grandparents or elders how they got water and stored it, and whether they used it the way we do today. You can write a short story about what you find out. Many years ago there were no pipes or taps anywhere, so people learned to make vessels to store water. Put up an exhibition in the classroom of the water vessels you draw, and observe how many kinds there are and whether the vessels have patterns on them.
Water comes down to earth as rain, slowly fills streams, rivers, ponds, lakes, wells and groundwater, and from these sources we bring it home, store it and use it in many ways. Water helps keep things clean, which is very important for our health, but afterwards it becomes dirty water. Let us reduce our use of water and reuse it whenever possible, to take care of this precious gift.
Write a few lines about what you observed in the rain and where the rainwater went. Write a few lines about a stream, river, well, pond or lake near you: is it used for drinking, how does the water reach your home, and if it is not used, why not? Draw your birdbath and write the names of the birds and insects that come to drink. With your group, list the activities at home or outside that waste or pollute water, and think of three solutions to avoid wastage.

problem.en: Where does the water in a well come from?

text.en: Rainwater soaks into the soil.

why.en: Water goes down into the ground.

text.en: Some of it stays between the rocks and soil as underground water.
The well is dug to reach this water.

why.en: Water from the ground fills the well.

problem.en: Give three ways to save water at home.

text.en: Close the tap while brushing the teeth.
Reuse the water used for washing vegetables for plants.
Fix leaking taps.

why.en: A drip adds up to many litres.

prompt.en: Explain how rainwater reaches our taps and wells.

requiredIdeas.en: Rain falls and soaks into the soil
Pipes bring water to tanks and taps
Ways to save and reuse water

commonMisconceptions.en: Rain water comes from the tap

points.en: Rain fills streams, rivers, ponds, lakes, wells and groundwater.
Water reaches our homes by pipes, wells, tankers or carrying.
We store water in vessels of many materials.
We should not waste water and should reuse it.
Every drop counts and everyone needs clean drinking water.
We can watch the rain and ask questions about how it falls and where it goes.
Water that sinks into the soil refills wells and helps plants, and we should reuse used water for plants.
Birdbaths, free drinking water and saving every drop are small actions that care for water.
